content: 1. The primary objectives of auditing and reviewing stillbirths and neonatal deaths are to understand the burden of these events by analyzing trends over time, to identify causes of death and modifiable factors through detailed examination of individual cases, and to use this information to guide preventive actions for the future. Additionally, it aims to ensure accountability and compel decision-makers to address the issue with appropriate attention and response. 2. A stillbirth is defined as the death of a fetus before birth in a baby weighing at least 1000 grams, or if weight is unavailable, at least 28 completed weeks of gestation, or a body length of at least 35 cm. For international comparisons, the ICD-10 uses a lower threshold of 500 grams, 22 completed weeks, or a body length of 25 cm. 3. Neonatal death refers to the death of a baby within the first 28 days of life. 4. A minimum set of perinatal indicators should be collected for every birth and death. These include maternal age, place of delivery, mode of delivery, birth weight, gestational age, and birth outcome. This data should be integrated into routine information systems. 5. Modifiable factors are circumstances that could have prevented a death if a different course of action had been taken. The term modifiable is preferred over avoidable or substandard to reduce blame and focus on opportunities for positive change. Approaches to classifying modifiable factors range from simple to complex analytical methods. 6. Setting up a mortality audit at the facility level involves starting the process and adapting it as needed, rather than aiming for a perfect system on paper. This includes establishing a review committee, mobilizing resources, organizing data collection, and focusing on preventable cases. 7. The six-step cycle of auditing deaths at the facility level includes: Identifying cases for review by recording all births, stillbirths, and neonatal deaths, and deciding which deaths require detailed review. Collecting standardized information from patient files or registers as soon as possible after a death. Analyzing the data to identify systemic problems contributing to stillbirths and neonatal deaths, particularly preventable ones. Recommending specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, and time-bound solutions to address identified problems. Implementing solutions through immediate, medium-term, or long-term actions to prevent future deaths. Evaluating the process and outcomes to refine future recommendations and ensure they lead to actionable changes. 8. Reporting audit findings is crucial for disseminating key messages to those who can implement changes. Reports should be clear, straightforward, and avoid placing blame on patients, clinicians, or teams. They should include data trends, case studies, and follow-up actions. 9. Community involvement in mortality audits plays two important roles: Capturing deaths that occur in the community, which may differ from those in health facilities, to provide a complete picture of why deaths occur and how they can be prevented. Ensuring community ownership of actions by engaging community members in identifying locally appropriate solutions and addressing barriers to care. 10. Leadership is essential in creating an enabling environment for mortality audits. Leaders should foster a culture of accountability, correction, celebration, and encouragement. Clear roles and responsibilities for various stakeholders, including health professionals, managers, and community liaisons, should be established. 11. Legal protection is critical for ensuring confidentiality and separating death review meetings from criminal investigations or disciplinary processes. Administrators should seek legal counsel early in the process to protect staff and patients. 12. Each death reviewed provides an opportunity to learn what could have been done differently to improve outcomes for mothers and babies. There is increasing demand for guidance on implementing and scaling up mortality audits as part of quality improvement strategies. 13. Leaders must champion the process, ensure a no-blame environment, and address systemic concerns. The benefits of audit and feedback in preventing maternal deaths are well-recognized and should also be applied to prevent neonatal deaths. 14. Tools and forms available for mortality audits include standardized audit forms, perinatal indicator checklists, systems for classifying modifiable factors, review committee guidelines, meeting codes of practice, calculation worksheets, and templates for meeting minutes. These resources support the implementation and tracking of mortality audits.
